story.title: Kazakhstan Holds Parliamentary Election Amidst Tight Control
story.summary: Kazakhstan has conducted a parliamentary election in which only state-approved parties loyal to President Tokayev were allowed to participate. This election is expected to further solidify the president's power following a significant constitutional overhaul. Opposition parties were banned from taking part in the electoral process.

explore_lenses.label: What changed in Kazakhstan’s political system?
explore_lenses.title: A new one-chamber legislature with expanded presidential leverage
explore_lenses.summary: The election fills the new Kurultai, created by the 2026 constitutional overhaul. The changes preserve legislative functions for the new chamber but give the president substantial appointment and agenda-setting authority.

claims.text: The new Kurultai has 145 deputies, elected for five-year terms by proportional representation in one nationwide electoral district.

The constitution gives the president authority, with Kurultai consent, to appoint the vice president, prime minister, Constitutional Court judges, Central Election Commission members and Supreme Audit Chamber members; it also permits dissolution of the Kurultai after specified repeated refusals.

Tokayev said the overhaul was needed to enable rapid decisions amid geopolitical instability; AP reported that the March referendum also merged the former two chambers and restored the vice presidency.

Tokayev said the overhaul was needed to enable rapid decisions amid geopolitical instability; AP reported that the March referendum also merged the former two chambers and restored the vice presidency.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: How these constitutional powers will operate in practice depends on the new Kurultai’s composition and subsequent appointments.

explore_lenses.label: Which parties competed, and what do critics say?
explore_lenses.title: Seven registered party lists, with concerns over meaningful competition
explore_lenses.summary: The election authority registered seven party lists, while reporting from AP describes the leading party and expected entrants as aligned with Tokayev. A prominent independent journalist says pressure on independent media has intensified during the campaign.

claims.text: The Central Election Commission said seven parties registered lists containing 545 candidates for the 145 Kurultai seats: Adilet, Nationwide Social Democratic, Baitaq, People’s Party, Auyl, Ak Zhol and Respublica.

The CEC said election rules require equal rights for parties in access to designated campaign-material locations and voter-meeting venues; it also said the ban on photographing completed ballots is intended to protect secret voting and independent voter choice.

Independent journalist Lukpan Akhmedyarov told AP that repression of independent media, cyberattacks and criminal cases against journalists and bloggers had intensified before the vote, and that Adilet advertising dominated major-city streets.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the vote?
explore_lenses.title: The new Kurultai must organize and approve key appointments
explore_lenses.summary: Once its first session opens, the Kurultai begins its five-year term and will have immediate institutional tasks, including selecting a chairperson and considering presidential nominees for major posts.

claims.text: The Kurultai’s powers begin when its first session opens; the president convenes that first session, while deputies elect a chairperson by secret ballot from a candidate nominated by the president.

Within two months after the first session opens, the constitution requires the president to appoint a vice president with Kurultai consent and to make the appointments for the Constitutional Court, Central Election Commission and Supreme Audit Chamber under the new constitutional framework.

story_report.summary: Kazakhstan held a parliamentary election on August 23 in a contest limited to state-approved parties, a result expected to reinforce President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s hold on power. The vote was for a newly configured 145-seat Kurultai, whose members will serve five-year terms. Pro-presidential Adilet was widely expected to win an overwhelming majority, while smaller parties described as loyal to Tokayev were also expected to enter the legislature, potentially giving the president a supportive body for appointments under the revised constitution.

sections.heading: Kurultai Powers Under Constitutional Overhaul
sections.body: The new Kurultai is elected by proportional representation from a single nationwide electoral district. Under the constitution, the president can, with Kurultai consent, appoint the vice president, prime minister, Constitutional Court judges, Central Election Commission members and Supreme Audit Chamber members. The framework also allows the president to dissolve the Kurultai after specified repeated refusals. Tokayev said the overhaul was needed for rapid decision-making amid geopolitical instability; the March referendum merged the former two chambers and restored the vice presidency.

sections.heading: Party Registration and Campaign Conditions
sections.body: The Central Election Commission said seven parties registered lists containing 545 candidates for the 145 seats: Adilet, Nationwide Social Democratic, Baitaq, People’s Party, Auyl, Ak Zhol and Respublica. The commission said parties were entitled to equal access to designated campaign-material sites and voter-meeting venues. Independent journalist Lukpan Akhmedyarov, however, told AP that pressure on independent media had intensified before the vote, citing cyberattacks and criminal cases against journalists and bloggers, while Adilet advertising dominated major-city streets.

sections.heading: Kurultai Opening and Presidential Appointments
sections.body: The Kurultai’s powers begin when its first session opens, which the president convenes. Deputies will elect their chairperson by secret ballot from a candidate nominated by the president. Within two months of the opening, the constitution requires the president to appoint a vice president with Kurultai consent and make appointments for the Constitutional Court, Central Election Commission and Supreme Audit Chamber under the new framework.

unresolved.text: Final seat totals, turnout, any election challenges and the timing of the Kurultai’s first session had not been established in the consulted reporting as of August 23, when voting was underway.
The official registration record identifies the parties on the ballot but does not independently determine whether campaign conditions permitted genuinely competitive opposition politics.
How the revised constitutional powers will operate in practice depends on the new Kurultai’s composition and subsequent appointments.

related_stories.title: Trade War Erupts as US-Canada Talks Fail and Tariffs Are Imposed
related_stories.summary: Following the collapse of trade negotiations, US President Donald Trump criticized Canada for imposing retaliatory tariffs. He claimed that Canada seeks the advantages of being a US state without actually being one. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the tariffs, stating that the US initiated the trade conflict.

related_stories.title: Zelensky Faces Corruption Questions Amid Calls for Elections
related_stories.summary: Former Defence Minister of Ukraine has raised concerns about corruption within President Zelensky's government, stating that Zelensky has 'questions to answer.' The former minister also advocated for holding elections in Ukraine. In response, Zelensky expressed that conducting elections during wartime would be too dangerous and could further divide the country.

related_stories.title: Supreme Court Permits Continued Construction of $400M White House Ballroom
related_stories.summary: The Supreme Court has temporarily allowed construction of President Trump's White House ballroom to proceed, following a stay issued by Chief Justice John Roberts. This decision comes as the court considers an appeal from the Trump administration regarding the project, which is estimated to cost nearly $400 million and is funded by private donors and companies. The ruling prevents a halt to construction that would have been enforced by lower court decisions.
